div.head: The file and its header
div.p: A file is one document: a TEI root, TEI, in TEI's namespace, holding a header, teiHeader, the text, text, and, where the file lists records, relations or annotations, a standOff after the text. The header says what the document is, who made the file and from what, and how the text was encoded. Its skeleton is required: the title statement with its formal title, the publication statement, and the description of the source. The rest is common or full, as each section says.
The root needs no id: the document's code, in the formal title, identifies it. A root's xml:id is the encoder's, and the import doesn't read it.

div.head: The title statement
div.p: The title statement (titleStmt) opens with the formal title, title typed formal, which holds the document's identifiers, once each:

list.item: its code, an idno without a type ();
its category, an idno typed category;
its type, an idno typed type.

div.p: Its other titles follow: an alias, the title readers know it by, and titles typed other, each naming its source in source. The formal title and its three identifiers are required: the import needs the code for the document's id. The Schematron checks them as errors, which the import reports. An alias is common; other titles are full. The Council of Mainz, 813:

Identifiers in the title statement stand in the formal title, and are its code, its category, its type, or, in an export, the permalinks of the levels the document belongs to: one each for its work, its version, its witness and its transcription (). Those are export only: the application writes them.

div.head: Categories and types
div.p: The category says what kind of text the document is. The application keeps the categories as a vocabulary, which may grow; the schema checks them against its list, which these seed:

list.item: SYSCOLL: a collection arranged by subject;
CHRCOLL: a collection arranged chronologically;
C: a council;
D: a decretal;
P: a penitential;
H: a homiliary;
EX: exegesis;
EP: a letter, not a pope's;
LR: Roman law, lex Romana;
CPT: a capitulary;
CHA: a charter;
UNK: not known.

div.p: The type says what the file transcribes:

list.item: edition: a text as a scholarly edition prints it;
manuscript: a text as a manuscript gives it, transcribed from it; its source description is the manuscript's ();
reconstruction: a text that scholars have reconstructed from others, such as a collection known from parts of other collections;
hypothesis: any text supposed rather than found, less precise than a reconstruction;
placeholder: a text whose content stands in for another's, such as a manuscript's text taken for now from the edition that used it.

div.head: The coding rules
div.p: A document's code says what the document is: its category, its title, its date, and, where needed, its source. Codes are made by the rules below, from the old Solemne guide, revised. The Schematron checks the code's form and its prefix, that a manuscript's code goes with the manuscript's description, and that a file named by a code is named by its own; the rest of the rules are the project's practice, explained here and not checked. A tool that proposes codes may come later.
A code has up to three parts, joined by dots:

list.item: The category's prefix: the category itself (C, D, P, H, EX, EP, LR, CPT, CHA), and COLL for both kinds of collection. A document of an unknown category takes any prefix.

The source part, where the code would otherwise be another document's: ms- and the manuscript's short code, for every transcription of a manuscript (COLL.400.ms-Mun-BSB-4592); ed- and the edition, where the corpus holds two editions of one text: the volume of the Patrologia Latina (COLL.Burch.ed-PL140), SCTA's Gratian (COLL.Grat.ed-SCTA).

div.p: A manuscript's short code joins, by hyphens, its city in three letters, its library's abbreviation and its shelfmark: Mun-BSB-4592 for Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 4592. A code is a valid xml:id: ASCII letters and digits joined by dots and hyphens, without spaces, accents or parentheses, so a former shelfmark has no place in it. An underscore stands only in a pointer, before a citation ().
No file of the corpus has the categories LR, CPT or CHA yet. Their codes follow the general rule, with their own prefixes; how their title parts are made, the guide will say with the first files.
A file named by a code, whatever the category's, is named by its own: C.MAI-0813.xml. A file named otherwise isn't checked; one named by another code is reported. Only a whole file can show it:
The import gives the document the code as its id, read with its kind ().

div.head: Responsibility and funding
div.p: After its titles, the title statement may name who did what for the document: its editors, the scholars whose study it rests on, the cataloguer of its manuscript, its encoders. Each is a respStmt with what they did, resp, dated by when where known, and who, a persName or an orgName pointing to its record in ref (). A funder names who paid for the work. Both are full. The Council of Carthage of 397 names its editor and its funder:

The header points to records as the text does, by ref, in the same forms: a title to its work, an author or an editor to a person. key and corresp keep TEI's other uses; a record's pointer in them is reported. provenance, acquisition and origin, in a manuscript's description, have no ref in TEI: the record they point to is named inside them, by a name with ref, and the import makes the relation from that name.

constraintSpec.desc: A record is pointed to by @ref, not by @key or @corresp.

sch:rule.sch:report: <> points to a record in @key or @corresp (): a record is pointed to by @ref, on a name inside provenance, acquisition and origin.

div.head: Publication and source
div.p: The publication statement (publicationStmt) says who publishes the file, not its source: for the project's files, the project, with its address. It's required, and may be a paragraph:

publicationStmt.publisher: SOLEMNE: 'The Social Life of Early Medieval Normative Texts'

div.p: The source description (sourceDesc), also required, describes what the text was transcribed from: an edition, as a biblStruct (); a manuscript, as a manuscript description (); for a reconstruction, the editor's publication, with the witnesses it rests on in a listWit. The Council of Mainz, 813, from Werminghoff's edition:

div.head: How the text was encoded
div.p: The encoding description (encodingDesc) says, once for the file, what the text's encoding needs explained. All of it is full. In its editorial declaration (editorialDecl), a normalization says what the transcription normalised (); the sections below give the rest.

div.head: Inferred units
div.p: Where the encoder didn't mark the units of reception (), so that a division's paragraphs may be several units, a segmentation typed inferred-units says so, with a paragraph, which TEI requires. For the whole file, it is the default (default true) or stands alone. For a few divisions among many marked units, it has default false and an id, and those divisions point to it in decls; one that none points to is reported.

segmentation.p: The units of reception aren't marked in the chapters that point here: each paragraph may be one.
The units of reception aren't marked in some chapters: each is one.

div.head: Curation
div.p: How far a text has been checked is its curation: correction, in the editorial declaration, with its status, high, medium, low or unknown, and a paragraph saying how, which TEI requires. The whole text's is the default; a division or a paragraph whose text was checked otherwise points to another correction in decls. Of several, one is the default. A text's completeness is never stated: the application counts it from the gaps.

A file that states no curation is imported as medium, checked at least once, when it is one of the project's coded files, a file of the Patrologia Latina or SCTA's Gratian, and as low when it comes from handwritten text recognition. high is set in the application, node by node. What was left out by choice is said once, in samplingDecl.
Placuit ut episcopi in ciuitatibus suis maneant.

div.head: Other projects' ids
div.p: A node's ids in other projects, SCTA's resources, the Clavis canonum's keys, Corpus Corporum's sections, go in sameAs, on the division or the paragraph, each with a prefix declared in the header by a prefixDef in listPrefixDef, which turns it into an address. The application knows four:

list.item: scta, SCTA: http://scta.info/resource/$1;
clavis, the Clavis canonum: https://data.mgh.de/databases/clavis/db/legacysearch?key=$1;
corpuscorporum, Corpus Corporum's Patrologia Latina: https://mlat.uzh.ch/browser/$1;
pseudoisidor, the Pseudoisidor project, whose address the guide gives when a file first carries its ids.

div.p: Any other prefix may be declared, and is reported; a prefix used without its declaration is an error. A Clavis key on a chapter:

A text of the Patrologia Latina has Corpus Corporum's id, cps_2. (its corpus 2, the Patrologia Latina) and the text's id there; a paragraph adds :, its division's position, ; and its position among the division's children, counted from 1 with the heading. For Absalon of Lund's Testamentum, PL 209, the text is corpuscorporum:cps_2.AbsLun.Testam17 and a paragraph corpuscorporum:cps_2.AbsLun.Testam17:3;16. The converter from PL's files writes them, on the text and on each paragraph that is one of the application's nodes; an encoder doesn't.

div.head: Calendars and vocabularies
div.p: The calendars and eras a file's dates use are declared once, and each date points to its own (). An export declares the terms of the application's vocabularies it uses, in classDecl, each with its permalink (); a file may declare terms too, such as a segment's ().

div.head: The abstract
div.p: The profile description (profileDesc) may hold an abstract: what the document is, its context, and what the file leaves out of it. It's full, and the import keeps it as the document's description. The Council of Aachen of 836:

abstract.p: Note that edition also contains a preface to this council, which has been omitted here.

div.head: The history of the file
div.p: The revision description (revisionDesc) lists the file's changes, the latest first, each a change with its date in when and who made it in who. The import keeps it as the file gives it, read-only, as the history before the import. An export writes the application's releases and a summary of the changes since the last, and, on request, each change set (). It's full. The Council of Carthage of 397:
